title: How to Get More Google Reviews for Your Restaurant in India
description: Get more genuine Google reviews for your restaurant in India: review QR codes, staff scripts, replying to bad reviews, reporting fakes and rules to avoid.
keywords: Google reviews for restaurant, get more Google reviews, restaurant review QR code, reply to negative Google reviews, remove fake Google reviews, Google review policy India, restaurant reputation management
body_html:
Your Google rating is often the first number a hungry customer sees. It sits next to your name on Google Search and Maps, before your menu, before your photos and long before your Swiggy or Zomato page. A restaurant with 40 recent, detailed reviews looks alive; one with eight reviews from 2022 looks closed, even if the food is excellent.

This guide shows Indian restaurants, cafés, QSRs and cloud kitchens how to get more genuine Google reviews every week, how to reply to them (especially the angry ones), how to get fake or abusive reviews removed, and which "growth hacks" can get your profile penalised. Every rule here comes from Google's own help and policy pages, read on the date of publishing and linked at the end. Google changes its tools often, so treat your own dashboard as the final word. If you have not set up your profile yet, start with our Google Business Profile setup checklist, and for the bigger picture see the 8 channels that bring restaurant customers in India.

Why Google reviews matter for a restaurant

Google says reviews show next to your Business Profile on Maps and Search, so every person who finds you there sees your rating and recent reviews. Reviews do more than decorate the listing. They answer the questions diners actually have: is the biryani spicy, is there parking, is it good for a family dinner, how long did delivery take. Google's own tips page makes a point worth remembering: "A mix of positive and negative feedback often feels more trustworthy." A wall of identical five-star reviews is not the goal. A steady flow of honest, specific reviews is.

Google is also policing reviews far more actively than a few years ago. In its April 2026 Maps safety update, Google said that in 2025 it blocked or removed over 292 million policy-violating reviews, removed over 13 million fake Business Profiles and placed posting restrictions on more than 782,000 accounts. Shortcuts that may have worked once are now a real risk to your listing.

The rules: what you can and cannot do

Google's Maps content policy explicitly allows businesses to ask for reviews, as long as they do it "without offering incentives to do so or attempting to influence the rating or the contents of the review." Here is how that plays out in a restaurant.

AllowedNot allowed
Asking every guest for a review, in person, on the bill or by messageAsking only happy guests ("selectively solicit positive reviews", known as review gating)
A table tent or counter standee with your review QR codePressuring guests to post a review while they are still on the premises
Thanking reviewers and replying to every reviewDiscounts, free desserts, cashback or any other incentive in exchange for a review
Fixing a complaint and letting the guest decide whether to update their reviewOffering anything to get a negative review changed or removed
Training staff to mention reviews politelyGiving staff a target number of reviews, or asking for reviews that mention specific dishes or words
Reporting reviews that break Google's policiesReviews by owners, staff, family or friends (Google treats these as conflict of interest), or reviews posted from multiple accounts

Two points catch many Indian outlets out. First, the common "show us your 5-star review and get a free mocktail" offer is exactly what Google calls fake engagement: its help page on review links says offering free or discounted goods or services in exchange for reviews is "strictly prohibited." Second, Google's policy lists "Merchants requesting that staff solicit a certain number of reviews" as prohibited, so a monthly review target for captains is a bad idea even if no customer gets a discount.

The penalties are visible to customers. Google's restrictions page says that for fake engagement, it may block your profile from receiving new reviews for a set period, unpublish your existing reviews for a set period, and display a warning telling customers that fake reviews were removed. Google says it emails owners before applying a restriction and that businesses can appeal.

India's rules point the same way. In November 2022 the Department of Consumer Affairs and the Bureau of Indian Standards launched IS 19000:2022, "Online Consumer Reviews — Principles and Requirements for their Collection, Moderation and Publication". BIS says it applies to any organisation that publishes consumer reviews online, including sellers of products and services that collect reviews from their own customers. The government said it would initially be voluntary, and that if made mandatory, violations could be treated as an unfair trade practice under consumer law. If you publish reviews on your own website, read the standard's principles on the BIS and PIB pages linked below. This is general information, not legal advice.

Step 1: Get your review link and QR code

Google now gives every verified profile a ready-made review link and QR code. According to Google's help page:

  1. Open your Business Profile (sign in at business.google.com or search your restaurant name on Google while signed in).
  2. Select Read reviews, then Get more reviews.
  3. Select Copy to copy the link, or right-click the QR code and choose Save image as.

Google notes that review QR codes can currently be generated only on a computer browser, not on a phone, so do this once on a laptop and save the image. Your profile must be verified before you can reply to reviews, so finish verification first.

One practical detail: Google says customers must be signed in to a Google Account to leave a review. Most Android users already are, but older guests or iPhone users may not be. That is why a QR code that opens straight onto the review box works better than "please search for us on Google".

Step 2: Put the ask where guests already look

Google suggests putting the link on receipts, in thank-you emails, at the end of chats and as a printed QR code in your store. Translated into an Indian restaurant's touchpoints:

  • The printed bill. Every dine-in and takeaway guest reads it. If your billing software lets you add a custom footer or QR code, put the review QR and one short line there: "Enjoyed your meal? Tell others on Google."
  • Table tents and the billing counter. A small standee at the cash counter and on each table. Keep it separate from your menu QR if you use Table QR ordering, and label it clearly so guests do not scan the wrong one.
  • Delivery packaging. A small insert or sticker with the QR code on orders from your own website. On aggregator orders, check the platform's rules on inserts first.
  • WhatsApp and SMS. Google's help page itself suggests sending the review link by WhatsApp or email. Send it only to guests who have shared their number and agreed to hear from you, and send it to everyone you message, not just guests you think are happy.
  • Your own website. Add a "Review us on Google" link on the order-confirmation page of your online ordering website.
  • Instagram. An occasional story with the link, especially after a busy weekend or a festival menu.

Step 3: Train staff to ask the right way

The single biggest lever is a polite, consistent spoken ask. A script that stays inside Google's rules:

"Thank you for coming today. If you have a minute later, we'd really value a Google review, good or bad. The QR code is on your bill."

Notice what the script avoids. It does not ask for five stars, does not mention a dish to praise, does not offer anything and does not ask the guest to do it at the table. It invites honest feedback from everyone. Give your captains this one line, and remove any review targets or incentives tied to review counts. Recognise good service in other ways.

Timing matters. The natural moments are when the bill is presented, when a regular compliments the food, or after you have resolved a problem well. Avoid asking a guest who is clearly unhappy to "please review us" before you have fixed the issue. Fix it first; the review is their choice.

Step 4: Reply to every review, the right way

Google's tips page is direct: "Your replies are public." Replies are reviewed against Google's policies before they appear; Google says this usually takes up to 10 minutes but can occasionally take up to 30 days. The reply shows as coming from your business, not your personal name, and the customer is notified. To reply, open your profile, select Read reviews, then Reply next to the review.

Google's guidance for replies boils down to:

  • Keep it short and simple.
  • Make each reply count. Do not paste the same "Thank you!" under every review.
  • Be conversational, not promotional. No offers or discount codes in replies.
  • Respond in a timely manner.
  • Address the reviewer by name and sign off with your name or initials.

Replying to a positive review

Mention something specific they said and invite them back. For example: "Thanks, Priya! Glad the Sunday thali hit the spot. The Kolkata-style mutton returns on the 1st. See you soon. – Rahul, Manager." (Illustrative example.)

Replying to a negative review

Google's advice for negative reviews: never share a reviewer's private information or make personal attacks; if the issue is complex, ask the reviewer to contact you by phone or email; be honest and explain limitations without taking responsibility for things outside your control; and apologise when appropriate. A simple structure:

  1. Thank and acknowledge: "Thank you for telling us, Arjun. A 50-minute wait for starters is not acceptable."
  2. Explain briefly, without excuses: "We were short-staffed in the kitchen on Saturday night, and we should have told you the wait time upfront."
  3. Say what changed: "We now quote kitchen wait times at the table during peak hours."
  4. Take it offline: "Please call me at the outlet number on this profile so I can make this right. – Neha, Owner."

(Illustrative example.) What you must not do is offer a refund or free meal in exchange for changing the review. You can resolve a genuine complaint, but Google's policy bans offering incentives for "revision or removal of a negative review". Google notes that customers can still edit their review after reading your reply, and if they do, the review date updates. Leave that decision to them.

For delivery complaints that are really about the aggregator (late rider, wrong order routed by the app), reply politely, explain what you control, and fix the kitchen side. Keeping orders from Swiggy, Zomato and your own channels in one system, as with a Swiggy and Zomato POS integration, makes it easier to check what actually happened to an order before you reply.

Step 5: Report fake, abusive or off-topic reviews

Google is clear that you can report any review, but only reviews that break its policies are eligible for removal. It "doesn't get involved in conflict between businesses and customers", so a harsh but genuine one-star review will stay. Reviews that may qualify include spam, profanity, reviews from competitors or people with a conflict of interest, content not based on an experience at your location, and general rants or political commentary.

  1. From your profile, open Read reviews, select Report on the review, pick a reason and send.
  2. Google says evaluation "typically takes several days". Track the status in Google's Reviews Management Tool.
  3. If the status shows "Report reviewed - no policy violation", you get a one-time appeal. You can appeal up to 10 reviews at once from the tool, and Google emails the final decision.

Watch for review extortion. In April 2026 Google described scams where people post fake one-star reviews and then demand payment to remove them. Google says that when it sees a sudden spike in spam reviews it will remove the fake content, pause new reviews on the profile, alert the owner and show a notification banner. Google also has a separate form to report negative-review extortion. Never pay; report it.

Worked example: what a review routine can add up to

The numbers below are purely illustrative, to show how the steps compound. Your results will differ by city, cuisine and guest mix; Google publishes no typical conversion rate.

ItemIllustrative figure
Dine-in and takeaway bills per month (mid-size café)2,400
Guests who see the review QR on the bill or tableAll of them
Assumed share who leave a review after a spoken ask plus QR1.5%
New reviews per monthAbout 36
Owner time to reply (2 minutes per review)About 72 minutes a month
One-time cost: 25 printed table tents and 2 counter standeesRoughly ₹2,000–₹3,000 (local print quotes vary)
Ongoing cost of a QR on every bill₹0 if your billing software prints it

The point of the example is the shape, not the figures: a small, steady ask across every guest beats a one-off push, costs very little, and keeps your reviews recent, which is what both Google and diners notice.

A weekly routine for the owner or manager

  • Daily (5 minutes): read new reviews and reply to each one, negative ones first.
  • Weekly: share recurring complaints (slow service, cold food, billing errors) with the kitchen and floor team. Check them against your sales and wastage reports to see if they match.
  • Weekly: check that the bill footer, table tents and counter QR still work and point to the right outlet.
  • Monthly: report any policy-violating reviews and check the Reviews Management Tool for decisions and appeals.
  • Every new staff member: teach the one-line script and the rules: no incentives, no targets, no asking only happy guests.

Multi-outlet brands should do this per outlet. Each location has its own profile and its own review link, so make sure every branch prints its own QR, not head office's. If you want billing, Table QR, online orders and reports for each outlet in one place, you can book a POSINEXT demo or compare plans; the routine above works with any POS.

faqs.question: Can I give customers a discount or free dessert for leaving a Google review?
faqs.answer: No. Google's policies ban offering payment, discounts, free goods or services in exchange for a review, or for changing or removing a negative one. Profiles caught doing this can have reviews removed, new reviews blocked and a warning shown to customers.

faqs.question: Is it allowed to ask only happy customers for Google reviews?
faqs.answer: No. Google's policy says businesses must not selectively solicit positive reviews or discourage negative ones. Ask every guest the same way and let them choose what to write.

faqs.question: How do I get a QR code for my restaurant's Google reviews?
faqs.answer: Open your Business Profile on a computer, select Read reviews, then Get more reviews, and save the QR code image. Google says review QR codes currently cannot be generated on a mobile device.

faqs.question: Can Google remove a negative review that I think is unfair?
faqs.answer: Only if it breaks Google's policies, for example spam, profanity, a conflict of interest or content not based on a real experience. Google does not remove genuine reviews just because a business disagrees. You can report a review and, if it is rejected, file a one-time appeal through the Reviews Management Tool.

faqs.question: How long does it take for my reply to a Google review to appear?
faqs.answer: Google checks replies against its policies first. It says this usually takes up to 10 minutes but can sometimes take up to 30 days, and the customer is notified once the reply is posted.

faqs.question: Can my staff or family write Google reviews for our restaurant?
faqs.answer: No. Google treats reviews from current or former employees, family members and others with a personal or professional connection as a conflict of interest, and removes them.
